paras: The lynching of the Tarno brothers was the hanging of three white men by a masked mob near Augusta, Arkansas, in the night of February 2-3, 1881. The men, accused of attempting to rape a young woman of the town, were taken from the jail, carried across the river and hanged, and their bodies were reportedly thrown into the river. A Little Rock wire dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within two days.

According to the Memphis Public Ledger, Miss Hamblett, daughter of a prominent Augusta merchant, was walking home from a neighbor's with a servant girl shortly after dark on Tuesday when three men ordered her to halt and chased her to her father's gate. The Ledger said the screams and 'the approach of a colored man' made the men flee, leaving her uninjured beyond the fright, while the Omaha Bee's version of the wire said her clothes were torn from her person. The wire reports dated the attack Wednesday.

The men were caught, and the officers had what the wire called 'a sharp fight' with a crowd crying 'Hang them!' 'Kill them!' before they lodged them in jail. Early dispatches said they were sons of wealthy Monroe County planters, while the Ledger named them as three brothers named Tarno, recently from Missouri. A later Chicago Times special gave their names as Robert, Jacob and a third brother whose name is garbled in print, sons of a wealthy man in a Missouri border county, and said they had been drinking for two or three days.

Around midnight or one o'clock, a mob of masked men, about twenty according to a New Orleans Democrat special, broke into the jail and bucked and gagged the jailer and guards. The mob took the prisoners by boat across the river to a grove of cottonwood and elm trees some distance from the opposite bank. There, by the Chicago Times account, a council was held, and accounts conflicted over whether the men admitted guilt and begged for mercy.

The same special said the brothers fought desperately, that half a dozen men were needed to hold them while they were bound and gagged, and that the ground afterward showed torn clothing and blood. They were hanged from the trees, and the wires reported that the bodies were then thrown into the river. The Ledger called that last detail 'hardly probable'.

No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage. The Chicago Times correspondent wrote, in a passage badly garbled in print, that public sentiment favored the lynchers and that no investigation or arrests were likely, the young woman's family being among the wealthiest in the state.

The story spread through a short Little Rock dispatch, reprinted from Lancaster to Omaha under headlines such as 'Lynched', 'Swift Retribution', 'Lynch Law in Arkansas' and 'A Prompt Lynching'. The wire called the accused 'the brutes' or 'the would-be rapists' and described the hanging as 'ghastly work', and one New Orleans special appeared in Richmond under a garbled 'Lime Rocks' dateline. Weekly papers reduced it to a line among other news, and the Arkansas Batesville Guard spoke of 'a most atrocious assault'.

The Memphis Public Ledger gave the fullest early account, centered on the young woman, who was known in Memphis as the sister of Mrs. Josie Harry, namesake of a river steamer. It endorsed the lynching's logic, writing that 'respectable people will submit no longer to the uncertain results of the laws' and sought 'summary vengeance through the aid of Judge Lynch'. The Chicago Times special, reprinted in Dakota under 'A Terrible Lynching', dwelt on the struggle and described the lynchers as yelling 'like demons' as their victims died.

The dates vary: a dispatch dated February 3 already reported the lynching as 'last night', and the Batesville Guard placed it on the night of the 2d, while a February 4 wire put it at one o'clock that morning. The Memphis Daily Appeal placed Augusta in White county, whereas other papers mentioned Monroe County only as the home of the men's fathers.

reader.title: Lynching of the Tarno brothers
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A masked mob took three jailed men accused of attempted rape from the Augusta jail, carried them across the river and hanged them (A1, A7, A20).

A mob of 'about twenty' masked men overpowered the jailer and guards and hanged three prisoners for an alleged attempted rape (A3, A6, A1); the Memphis Public Ledger framed it as 'summary vengeance through the aid of Judge Lynch' (A8). The victims were described as 'three white men' (A7, A9), so this was not anti-Black violence.

The Little Rock wire (A1, A3, A7), a separate Little Rock Gazette-based account in the Memphis Public Ledger (A8), an Arkansas weekly (A15) and a Chicago Times special (A20) agree on the seizure from jail and the hanging across the river.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire
accounts.gist: Three men attempted to rape Miss Hamblet, were captured after the officers fought a crowd to jail them, and a masked mob gagged the jailer, hanged them across the river and threw the bodies in the water.

accounts.label: Memphis Public Ledger (citing Little Rock Gazette special)
accounts.gist: The men accosted Miss Hamblett and a servant girl after dark on Tuesday, fled when a 'colored man' approached, and were caught; they were three brothers named Tarno from Missouri; she was 'uninjured'; the report of bodies in the river was 'hardly probable'.

accounts.label: Chicago Times special from Little Rock
accounts.gist: The brothers had been drinking for days; the mob held a council in a grove across the river, the men resisted desperately and were bound, gagged and hanged, and the bodies were dragged to the river; accounts conflicted on whether they confessed.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Little Rock dispatch as a crime brief, calling the men 'the brutes' or 'the would-be rapists' and the killing 'ghastly' or 'horrible work'.
The Memphis Public Ledger said 'respectable people will submit no longer to the uncertain results of the laws' and sought 'summary vengeance through the aid of Judge Lynch'.
The Chicago Times special, headed 'A Terrible Lynching', called the men 'debased' and the assault 'brutal' but described the lynchers as yelling 'like demons'.

conflicts.note: The earliest dispatch, dated Little Rock Feb. 3, already reports the lynching as 'last night' (A3), which supports the night of Feb. 2-3.
The Feb. 4 wires probably carried over 'yesterday' from the Feb. 3 dispatch.

Seized from the jail at Augusta, Ark.; hanged on trees on the opposite bank of the river, in a grove of cottonwood and elm 'some distance from the opposite bank'.
Three men, called 'three white men'; named as three brothers Tarno (Robert, a garbled second name, and Jacob), said to be recently from Missouri, or sons of wealthy Monroe County planters.
Accused of attempting to rape or 'outrage' Miss Georgia/Georgiana/Georgie Hamblet(t), daughter of an Augusta merchant.
A mob or 'company' of masked men; 'a party of citizens of Augusta'; 'a crowd of infuriated citizens'.
